ECE 6612

IP security, tunnels and network visibility

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows an IPsec tunnel protecting an inner packet between gateways while an outer IP header routes it across the network.

IP supplies routing addresses and packet delivery without built-in authentication of the sender’s claimed source address. IPv4 has 32-bit addresses; IPv6 has 128-bit addresses. A prefix /r fixes the first r bits, leaving 2^(w−r) addresses in a w-bit address space before any address-use reservations. A source address therefore describes a claimed return location; cryptographic authentication or network enforcement supplies stronger evidence.

IPsec adds security associations containing keys, algorithms, sequence handling and policy for protected traffic. Encapsulating Security Payload, or ESP, can provide confidentiality and integrity according to the chosen suite. Authentication Header, or AH, supplies authentication over specified packet fields without encrypting the data. Internet Key Exchange, or IKE, negotiates authenticated key establishment and association parameters. The configured peer identities and accepted credentials determine who can establish protection. An authenticated ESP sequence number and an anti-replay window can reject duplicates and packets outside the receiver’s accepted range for that association.

In transport mode, ESP protects the transport payload while the original outer IP header remains available for routing. In tunnel mode, ESP protects an entire inner IP packet and a new outer IP header identifies the tunnel endpoints. A site-to-site tunnel therefore protects the gateway-to-gateway span. The original hosts’ paths to their gateways need their own protections if the same confidentiality goal extends there.

A remote-access VPN similarly shifts which intermediary observes traffic. The local network sees the VPN connection and its traffic pattern; the VPN endpoint can see the traffic after its tunnel protection ends, including destination metadata. Application TLS may remain encrypted through that provider. In a chain, provider one terminates its tunnel before forwarding into provider two’s tunnel. With nested tunnels, the client creates an inner tunnel carried inside an outer one. Fig. 2 traces which endpoint removes each layer. Independence, collusion, routing and endpoint configuration determine the resulting visibility.

Source-address validation constrains spoofing at network boundaries. A customer-facing router can admit only source prefixes that customer may legitimately send, and a network’s outbound policy can enforce its permitted source ranges. Filtering depends on topology: asymmetric routing and multihoming require care when choosing reverse-path checks. A NAT mapping or an IPv6 address length supplies no replacement for a deliberate firewall policy; both protocol stacks need appropriate protection. Although a large IPv6 address space makes blind exhaustive scanning costly, DNS names, predictable address patterns and observed traffic can reveal active addresses. Attackers can also stress finite per-address tracking or neighbor-cache entries by triggering work for many addresses.

ICMP supplies diagnostics and errors, including Echo replies, Time Exceeded and Packet Too Big messages. Traceroute sends probes with increasing TTL or hop limit; expiring probes can trigger replies that reveal portions of the path. The timing measures that probe’s round trip, including return routing and device response behavior. A missing reply may reflect filtering or rate limits. Selective ICMP handling preserves useful functions such as path-MTU discovery while controlling unwanted traffic.

Example

A gateway tunnel carries a packet from inner source 192.0.2.10 to inner destination 198.51.100.20. An observer between gateways sees the outer gateway addresses and encrypted payload size/timing. After the exit gateway decrypts the inner packet, it can forward using the inner destination. TLS inside that packet keeps its application data protected until the TLS endpoint.

Sources and scope
  • Course scope: Network Layer Security, including IPsec, source validation, IPv6 and ICMP; tunnel visibility extension.
  • RFC 4301: IPsec architecture.
  • RFC 4303: ESP transport and tunnel mode.
  • RFC 7296: IKEv2.
  • RFC 2827 / BCP 38: network ingress filtering.
  • RFC 8201: IPv6 path-MTU discovery.

Practice

1. A company encrypts traffic only between its two office gateways using ESP tunnel mode. Which addresses must remain visible between those gateways, and which span needs an additional protection decision?

Follow the routing header before decryption and then the path inside each office.

The outer source and destination gateway addresses remain visible so routers can deliver the tunnel packet. The inner addresses and payload can be encrypted by ESP. The host-to-gateway paths inside each office fall outside this gateway tunnel’s protection and need their own protection decisions, such as trusted local links or application TLS.

2. A traceroute probe expires at hop 4 and receives an ICMP Time Exceeded response after 24 ms. What does that number measure, and what does an absent response from hop 5 establish?

Include the return path and the device’s choice to answer.

24 ms measures the elapsed round trip from sending that probe to receiving that ICMP response, including forward travel, response processing and return travel. An absent hop-5 response establishes that no response arrived within the observation window. Filtering, rate limiting, loss, return-path behavior or the device’s response policy can all affect the observation.
